about: Speechform's lenses: for each kind of speech, three questions asked of that form (what the listener must bring, what the speaker must know to deliver its meaning, and what draws a listener in), each answered from the scholarship of oral forms, with elements the algorithm can find in a transcript. Each kind also has an arc: the stages its talk moves through, used to judge where a thread stands and what move comes next. Read by depth.py, steer.py and light/depth.js.

sources: John Sweller, Cognitive Load Theory (working memory limits on spoken steps)
Walter J. Ong, Orality and Literacy (additive, situational oral organization)
Ruth Finnegan, Oral Literature in Africa (the practical genres of spoken instruction)
Aristotle, Rhetoric (arrangement and clarity of exposition)
Milton H. Erickson, The Collected Papers (pacing and leading with direct suggestion)

listener.question: What must a listener have in hand, or in mind, to follow spoken instructions?
listener.answer: A listener needs to know the goal of the task, the materials or setting it assumes, and where they stand in the sequence at each moment. John Sweller's cognitive load theory shows that spoken steps live in working memory, so the listener depends on the speaker to name each step and its order. Walter Ong describes oral organization as additive and situational, and instruction works best when it points at the things in front of the listener.

elements.name: Goal Named
elements.meaning: The listener hears what the steps will achieve before or while they begin.
elements.try: Say in one sentence what the listener will have made or done when the steps are finished.

cue.re: \b(?:so that|in order to|the goal|you(?:'ll| will) (?:have|end up|get)|to make|to get|to fix|to set up|you want to|until you|as (?:realistically|evenly|smoothly) as)\b

elements.name: Materials
elements.meaning: The tools, ingredients or parts the task needs are named.
elements.try: Name each tool or material before the step that uses it.

elements.name: Addressed
elements.meaning: The listener is spoken to directly as the one who will act.
elements.try: Speak to the listener as you, the person whose hands will do this.

elements.name: Place in Order
elements.meaning: Ordinal and sequence words tell the listener where they are in the task.
elements.try: Mark each step with first, then, next or finally.

elements.name: Measures
elements.meaning: Amounts, times and sizes let the listener check their work.
elements.try: Give a number for how much, how long or how far.

speaker.question: What must the speaker know to deliver the goal of a procedure so the listener can carry it out?
speaker.answer: The speaker must hold the whole procedure and its purpose, then release it one action at a time in the order the hands will need it. Aristotle asks for clarity and fitting arrangement, and in instruction that means one verb leading each step. The speaker also anticipates mistakes and names the sign that a step has worked, so the listener can correct course alone.

elements.name: Action Verbs
elements.meaning: Each step begins with the verb the listener must perform.
elements.try: Begin each step with the action itself: cut, press, turn, pour.

elements.name: One Step Each
elements.meaning: Steps arrive one per sentence, short enough to hold in memory.
elements.try: Keep each sentence to a single action and stop before adding the next.

elements.name: Check Sign
elements.meaning: The speaker names what the listener should see, hear or feel when a step has worked.
elements.try: Tell the listener how they will know the step is done.

cue.re: \b(?:until|so (?:that|they)|you(?:'ll| will) (?:see|hear|feel|notice)|make sure|be sure|check (?:that|the)|note what|it should|evenly|stays below)\b

elements.name: Caution
elements.meaning: A warning prevents the most likely mistake.
elements.try: Name the one mistake people make here and how to avoid it.

elements.name: Reason
elements.meaning: A brief reason tells the listener why a step matters.
elements.try: Add a short because or so that after the step that seems arbitrary.

absorption.question: Which elements of the act and of the task most draw a listener into following instructions?
absorption.answer: Absorption in instruction is the flow Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi describes, where clear goals and immediate feedback let attention settle on the hands. Milton Erickson used the same structure of pacing and leading: describe what the listener is already doing, then lead the next small action. A steady cadence of short steps and concrete sensory checks keeps the listener inside the task.

elements.name: Steady Cadence
elements.meaning: Steps of similar length give the listening a regular pulse.
elements.try: Keep your steps about the same length so the listener can settle into the rhythm.

elements.name: Pacing and Leading
elements.meaning: The speaker matches what the listener is doing now, then leads the next action.
elements.try: Say what the listener has just done, then lead into the next step with now or then.

cue.re: \b(?:now that|once you(?:'ve| have)?|when you(?:'ve| have)|as you|while you|now)\b

elements.name: Hands On
elements.meaning: Concrete physical verbs keep the body engaged.
elements.try: Use verbs the hands can feel: hold, press, pull, brush.

elements.name: Sensory Check
elements.meaning: Sounds, colours and textures give feedback the listener can perceive.
elements.try: Point to what the listener will hear, see or feel as it changes.

elements.name: Direct Address
elements.meaning: Steady second person keeps the listener as the one acting.
elements.try: Keep saying you, so the listener stays the actor.

arc.name: Goal

cue.re: \b(?:you(?:'ll| will) (?:need|want|end up)|the goal|we(?:'re| are) going to|to make|in order to|so that you)\b

arc.move: Say what the finished result will be.

arc.name: Materials
arc.move: Name what the listener needs before starting.

arc.name: Steps
arc.move: Give the next step in order.

arc.name: Check
arc.move: Tell the listener how to know a step worked.

arc.name: Done

cue.re: \b(?:and that'?s it|you'?re done|that'?s all|finally|when it'?s (?:done|ready)|now you have)\b

arc.move: Say how the listener knows they are finished.

sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (ethos, logos and arrangement in exposition)
Walter J. Ong, Orality and Literacy (the lecture as secondary orality shaped by writing)
Wallace Chafe, Discourse, Consciousness, and Time (how spoken information flows in idea units)
Donald A. Bligh, What's the Use of Lectures? (attention and retention in lectures)
Jerome Bruner, Actual Minds, Possible Worlds (the paradigmatic mode of explanation)

listener.question: What must a listener bring to follow a lecture and take its knowledge away?
listener.answer: A lecture assumes the listener can hold a frame, the field and its question, while evidence accumulates inside it. Walter Ong calls the lecture a creature of literacy spoken aloud, so the listener benefits from knowing the key terms and the debate the speaker enters. Donald Bligh found that attention falls after about twenty minutes, so the listener also brings stamina and the habit of noting structure.

elements.name: Field Named
elements.meaning: The discipline or area of inquiry is named.
elements.try: Name the field and the question it asks before the first claim.

elements.name: Key Terms
elements.meaning: Technical terms are introduced as the vocabulary of the talk.
elements.try: Define one key term in plain words when you first use it.

elements.name: The Debate
elements.meaning: The listener is told what earlier thinkers have argued.
elements.try: Say what others have long believed before you add what is known now.

cue.re: \b(?:long debated|generally agree|have argued|it was believed|debate|consensus|first proposed|have long|remains (?:central|an active))\b

elements.name: Era and Scale
elements.meaning: Dates, centuries or magnitudes place the knowledge.
elements.try: Give the date, era or scale that places this knowledge.

speaker.question: What must the lecturer know to deliver the central finding so it stays with the listener?
speaker.answer: The lecturer must know the single finding the talk exists to deliver and arrange evidence toward it, as Aristotle advises when he ranks logos and arrangement. Wallace Chafe shows that speech moves one idea unit at a time, so the speaker signposts the plan and returns to the point. Ethos comes from naming the sources of evidence, and clarity comes from a summary the listener can repeat.

elements.name: Signposting
elements.meaning: The speaker announces the plan of the talk and its turns.
elements.try: Tell the listener what you will cover and in what order.

cue.re: \b(?:today (?:we|i) will|in this (?:session|lecture|talk)|we will (?:look|examine|review|turn)|i will (?:explain|summarize|turn)|turning to|before turning|let us (?:turn|look))\b

elements.name: Evidence
elements.meaning: Studies, data and findings support the claims.
elements.try: Name the study or data that supports your claim.

elements.name: Central Finding
elements.meaning: The main point is stated outright as the finding.
elements.try: State the central finding in one sentence, then repeat it at the end.

cue.re: \b(?:the central (?:finding|point|idea)|the main (?:finding|point)|the key (?:finding|point)|clear pattern|in summary|to summarize|this means)\b

elements.name: Consequences
elements.meaning: The speaker draws out what the finding implies.
elements.try: Say what follows from the finding for the listener's world.

elements.name: Measured Register
elements.meaning: Long, complete sentences carry qualified claims.
elements.try: Qualify your claim with the conditions under which it holds.

absorption.question: Which elements of the lecture and of the material most absorb a listener in the line of thought?
absorption.answer: A lecture absorbs through the pleasure of a question opening and closing, which Jerome Bruner calls the paradigmatic mode carried by the drama of inquiry. Puzzles, surprising numbers and a story of discovery let the mind lean forward. A steady measured voice and recurring framing phrases work as gentle repetition, the device Milton Erickson used to deepen attention.

elements.name: The Puzzle
elements.meaning: A question or mystery in the material makes the listener want the answer.
elements.try: Pose the question the research set out to answer before giving the answer.

elements.name: Discovery Story
elements.meaning: The history of how the knowledge was found gives it a narrative line.
elements.try: Tell how the finding was discovered, in order, with who did what.

cue.re: \b(?:first proposed|was discovered|refined over|has been refined|began to|in the (?:\w+ )?century|over (?:several|many) decades|historians)\b

elements.name: Striking Number
elements.meaning: A vivid figure anchors attention.
elements.try: Give one surprising number and pause after it.

elements.name: Measured Pace
elements.meaning: Long, even sentences set a steady pace of thought.
elements.try: Let your sentences run at an even length so the listener can settle in.

elements.name: Frame Phrases
elements.meaning: Recurring scholarly framing returns the listener to the thread.
elements.try: Return to your framing phrase each time you add a new piece of evidence.

cue.re: \b(?:the evidence|the research|the theory|these studies|this concept|this theory|the data)\b

arc.name: Frame
arc.move: Frame the question this talk answers.

arc.name: Concept
arc.move: Name the central concept plainly.

arc.name: Evidence
arc.move: Bring the evidence that supports it.

arc.name: Implication
arc.move: Say why it matters.

arc.name: Summary

cue.re: \b(?:to sum up|in summary|to summari[sz]e|in short|the key (?:point|idea)|so (?:today|what we))\b

arc.move: Summarize the one thing to remember.

sources: Lev Vygotsky, Mind in Society (the zone of proximal development and scaffolding)
Paulo Freire, Pedagogy of the Oppressed (dialogue as the ground of learning)
Courtney Cazden, Classroom Discourse (the initiation, response and evaluation pattern)
Jerome Bruner, The Process of Education (scaffolding and discovery)
Plato, Meno (the Socratic question that leads the learner to find)

listener.question: What must a learner bring to take part in a spoken lesson?
listener.answer: A lesson asks the learner to be a participant, ready to answer, try and be corrected. Lev Vygotsky locates learning in the zone just beyond what the learner can do alone, so the learner brings what they already know and a willingness to stretch. Courtney Cazden shows that classroom talk runs in turns of question, response and evaluation, and learners who know that rhythm join in sooner.

elements.name: Invited In
elements.meaning: The learner is addressed and invited to take part.
elements.try: Speak to the learners as you and invite them in by name or by group.

elements.name: Class Setting
elements.meaning: Words of the classroom place the learner in a shared space.
elements.try: Name the shared space: the board, the page, the partner beside them.

elements.name: What They Know
elements.meaning: The lesson connects to something the learner already knows.
elements.try: Ask what they already know before you show the new thing.

cue.re: \b(?:remember (?:when|how)|you already|last time|we learned|you know|as we saw|which word|tell me)\b

elements.name: We Together
elements.meaning: Teacher and learners work as one group.
elements.try: Say let us or we to bring the group into the task together.

cue.re: \b(?:let'?s|we are going to|we'?re going to|together|we will)\b

speaker.question: What must the teacher know to deliver the takeaway so the learner owns it?
speaker.answer: The teacher must know the one thing the learner should be able to do by the end, and stage the lesson so the learner does it. Jerome Bruner names this scaffolding: model the task, share it, then hand it over. Socratic questioning, as in Plato's Meno, leads the learner to find the answer rather than receive it, and timely praise confirms each step.

elements.name: Model It
elements.meaning: The teacher demonstrates one example first.
elements.try: Do the first example aloud while they watch.

cue.re: \b(?:watch (?:how|me)|here is an example|look at the first|i'?ll do|the first one|for example|example on the board)\b

elements.name: Hand It Over
elements.meaning: The learner tries the next example alone.
elements.try: Hand the next one to the learners with now you try.

cue.re: \b(?:now you|you try|try (?:the next|it|this|the second)|on your own|yourselves|your turn)\b

elements.name: Checking Question
elements.meaning: Questions check understanding at each step.
elements.try: Ask a question that shows whether they have it.

elements.name: Feedback
elements.meaning: The teacher confirms and praises correct answers.
elements.try: Answer each attempt with a word of feedback such as good or exactly.

elements.name: Explain Why
elements.meaning: Learners are asked to explain their reasoning.
elements.try: Ask them to explain their answer to a partner.

cue.re: \b(?:explain|why do you think|how do you know|show (?:the class|me)|tell me (?:which|why|what))\b

absorption.question: Which elements of the lesson and of the task most draw learners into absorbed practice?
absorption.answer: Learners become absorbed when the task is just hard enough and the turns come quickly, the balance of challenge and skill that Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi calls flow. Paulo Freire places learning in dialogue, so questions that hand the floor to the learner keep attention alive. A brisk rhythm of call and response, like the call and response of oral traditions, sustains the group.

elements.name: Call and Response
elements.meaning: Questions and answers alternate quickly.
elements.try: Ask, wait for the answer, and answer back in a quick rhythm.

elements.name: Noticing
elements.meaning: Learners are asked what they notice or see.
elements.try: Ask what they notice before you explain anything.

elements.name: Safe to Try
elements.meaning: The teacher makes it safe to guess.
elements.try: Tell them a guess is welcome and wrong answers help.

cue.re: \b(?:take a guess|no wrong answers|have a go|try it|it'?s okay|give it a try|just try)\b

elements.name: Brisk Turns
elements.meaning: Short sentences keep the pace moving.
elements.try: Keep your sentences short so the turns come fast.

elements.name: Practice Now
elements.meaning: The lesson moves into doing.
elements.try: Give them a problem to work on right now.

arc.name: Hook
arc.move: Open with a question the class can answer.

arc.name: Example
arc.move: Show one worked example.

arc.name: Practice
arc.move: Hand the next one to the learners.

arc.name: Takeaway

cue.re: \b(?:so (?:remember|the rule)|the (?:rule|key|lesson) is|what we learned|today you learned|remember that)\b

arc.move: State the takeaway in one sentence.

sources: Deborah Tannen, Talking Voices (repetition and involvement in conversation)
H. P. Grice, Logic and Conversation (cooperative principle and implicature)
Harvey Sacks, Emanuel Schegloff and Gail Jefferson, A Simplest Systematics for the Organization of Turn-Taking for Conversation
Mikhail Bakhtin, The Dialogic Imagination (every utterance answers another)
Plato, Dialogues (the question and answer as a way of thinking together)

listener.question: What must a listener know to follow and enjoy a dialogue between voices?
listener.answer: A listener must track who is speaking and what each voice wants, often from the turns alone. Sacks, Schegloff and Jefferson show that conversation is built from turns that answer one another, so the listener follows the pairing of question and reply. Grice adds that speakers mean more than they say, and the listener enjoys dialogue by reading those implications.

elements.name: Turn Taking
elements.meaning: Questions are met by answers in alternating turns.
elements.try: Let one voice ask and the other answer, back and forth.

elements.name: Two Voices
elements.meaning: Both I and you are present as speakers.
elements.try: Let each speaker say I and address the other as you.

elements.name: Reference Back
elements.meaning: A speaker refers to what the other just said.
elements.try: Have a speaker quote or point back to the other's words.

cue.re: \b(?:you said|you mean|what did you mean|i meant|i thought you|that'?s what|you asked)\b

elements.name: Direct Reply
elements.meaning: Short replies like yes, no, oh and really mark responses.
elements.try: Begin a reply with yes, no, oh or really.

speaker.question: What must the speakers know to carry the point of a dialogue through its turns?
speaker.answer: Each speaker must know what they want from the exchange and let it show through what they ask and refuse. Mikhail Bakhtin teaches that every utterance answers another, so meaning lives in the response more than in any single line. Grice's cooperative principle explains why an unexpected answer lands, because the listener works out what the speaker implied.

elements.name: What Each Wants
elements.meaning: Speakers state wishes, needs and intentions.
elements.try: Let each speaker say what they want or mean to do.

cue.re: \b(?:i want|i wanted|i need|i'?d like|you wanted|i meant|i asked because|i'?ll come|let'?s go)\b

elements.name: Agreement
elements.meaning: Speakers agree, concede or push back.
elements.try: Let one speaker agree with part and push back on the rest.

cue.re: \b(?:i agree|i hear you|but|i disagree|of course|fair enough|you'?re right|i know)\b

elements.name: The Answer
elements.meaning: A question receives an explicit answer.
elements.try: Let the key question get a plain answer.

elements.name: Resolution
elements.meaning: The exchange arrives at a shared decision.
elements.try: End the exchange with what the two decide together.

elements.name: Implied Meaning
elements.meaning: Speakers imply more than they say through hedges and turns.
elements.try: Let one reply say less than it means and trust the listener to hear it.

absorption.question: Which elements of the exchange and of the situation most draw a listener into a dialogue?
absorption.answer: Deborah Tannen shows that repetition and quick rhythm in conversation create involvement, so listeners feel inside the exchange. Tension between what the voices want, and the pull of an unanswered question, holds attention from turn to turn. Short lines and quick returns work like the call and response of ballad and work song.

elements.name: Quick Turns
elements.meaning: Short lines pass quickly between voices.
elements.try: Shorten the lines so the voices answer each other fast.

elements.name: Open Question
elements.meaning: A question hangs in the air and pulls the next turn.
elements.try: Leave one question hanging for the other voice to answer.

elements.name: Echo
elements.meaning: Speakers echo each other's words.
elements.try: Let one speaker repeat a word the other used.

elements.name: Tension
elements.meaning: A disagreement or surprise sharpens the exchange.
elements.try: Let one voice resist or surprise the other.

elements.name: Address
elements.meaning: The voices speak straight to each other.
elements.try: Have the speakers address each other directly.

arc.name: Opening
arc.move: Open with a question to the other person.

arc.name: Exchange
arc.move: Answer what was just asked, then ask back.

arc.name: Tension
arc.move: Name where you differ.

arc.name: Settle
arc.move: Agree on what happens next.

sources: Jerome Bruner, Acts of Meaning (narrative as the making of the self)
Dan P. McAdams, The Stories We Live By (redemption sequences in life stories)
Donald A. Schön, The Reflective Practitioner (reflection on action)
William Labov, Language in the Inner City (evaluation in personal narrative)
Pauline Oliveros, Deep Listening (listening inward as practice)

listener.question: What must a listener bring to receive a reflective monologue with care?
listener.answer: A listener must be willing to hold someone else's memory and its meaning without hurrying it. Jerome Bruner argues that we make ourselves through the stories we tell about our past, so the listener receives a self being made. It helps to know the then and the now, the time remembered and the vantage from which the speaker looks back.

elements.name: Then and Now
elements.meaning: The speaker marks a past time and the present vantage.
elements.try: Name when it happened and where you stand now.

cue.re: \b(?:back then|at the time|in those years|those years|looking back|now i|now,? i|years later|i used to|when i was)\b

elements.name: First Person
elements.meaning: The speaker speaks as I about their own life.
elements.try: Speak as I and stay with your own experience.

elements.name: Memory Anchor
elements.meaning: A remembered place, person or object anchors the memory.
elements.try: Name one place or person the memory belongs to.

elements.name: Remembered Past
elements.meaning: The past tense carries the remembered events.
elements.try: Tell the remembered moment in the past tense.

speaker.question: What must the speaker know to deliver the meaning they have found in their own experience?
speaker.answer: The speaker must know what the experience taught them and state it as an understanding reached. William Labov calls this the evaluation, the part of a personal narrative that says why it matters. Dan McAdams finds that life stories carry meaning through turns from difficulty toward growth, and Donald Schön describes reflection on action as the source of practical wisdom.

elements.name: Realization
elements.meaning: The speaker states what they understand now.
elements.try: Say plainly what you understand now that you did not then.

cue.re: \b(?:i realize|i realized|i understand now|i've come to|i have come to|i see now|i learned|i know now|i came to see)\b

elements.name: Evaluation
elements.meaning: The speaker says why the experience matters.
elements.try: Tell the listener why this memory still matters to you.

cue.re: \b(?:taught me|grateful|it mattered|what it meant|i needed|the first (?:decision|time)|for myself|it gave me)\b

elements.name: Feeling Named
elements.meaning: The speaker names a feeling then and now.
elements.try: Name the feeling you had then and the one you have now.

elements.name: Turn in View
elements.meaning: The speaker shows how their view changed.
elements.try: Contrast how you saw it then with how you see it now.

cue.re: \b(?:differently|at the time i|now i (?:understand|see|know)|i never noticed|i thought .{0,30} but|though i never)\b

absorption.question: Which elements of the telling and of the memory chosen most draw a listener into reflection?
absorption.answer: Reflection absorbs when sensory memory makes the past present, the specific smell or sound that Milton Erickson used to invite listeners into their own recollections. A slow, inward voice invites the kind of attention Pauline Oliveros calls deep listening. The listener drifts into their own memories, which is the trance of reflection.

elements.name: Sensory Memory
elements.meaning: A remembered smell, sound or light makes the past vivid.
elements.try: Recall one smell, sound or light from the memory.

elements.name: Remembering
elements.meaning: Verbs of memory open the past.
elements.try: Begin with I remember and let the image follow.

cue.re: \b(?:i remember|i recall|i can still|looking back|i think about|when i think)\b

elements.name: Inward Voice
elements.meaning: The speaker turns inward with feeling words.
elements.try: Speak slowly about what was happening inside you.

elements.name: Quiet Place
elements.meaning: A still, intimate setting holds the memory.
elements.try: Place the memory in a small, quiet room or landscape.

arc.name: Memory

cue.re: \b(?:i remember|back then|when i was|years ago|at the time|i used to)\b

arc.move: Begin from a remembered moment.

arc.name: Feeling
arc.move: Say what it felt like then.

arc.name: Turn

cue.re: \b(?:but now|now i|looking back|i (?:have )?come to|i realize|i understand now|i see now)\b

arc.move: Turn from then to now.

arc.name: Meaning

cue.re: \b(?:it taught me|i learned|that'?s (?:how|why) i|it means|i am grateful|what (?:it|that) gave me)\b

arc.move: Say what it means to you now.

sources: K. Anders Ericsson and Herbert A. Simon, Protocol Analysis: Verbal Reports as Data
Donald A. Schön, The Reflective Practitioner (reflection in action)
Lev Vygotsky, Thought and Language (inner speech made audible)
Wallace Chafe, Discourse, Consciousness, and Time (hesitation and the flow of thought in speech)
George Pólya, How to Solve It (heuristics of problem solving)

listener.question: What must a listener bring to follow someone thinking aloud?
listener.answer: A listener must know the problem the speaker is trying to solve and be patient with false starts. Ericsson and Simon showed that thinking aloud reports the contents of attention as they pass, so the listener hears the path of a mind more than a finished answer. Vygotsky describes this as inner speech made audible, compressed and full of turns.

elements.name: Problem Stated
elements.meaning: The speaker names what they are trying to work out.
elements.try: Say what you are trying to work out before you begin.

cue.re: \b(?:let me think|think this through|the (?:problem|question) is|doesn'?t add up|don'?t add up|figure out|work out|how do i|what should i)\b

elements.name: First Person
elements.meaning: The speaker thinks as I.
elements.try: Keep speaking as I, from inside the problem.

elements.name: Options
elements.meaning: Possibilities are laid out to weigh.
elements.try: Lay out each option as a what if.

elements.name: Self Question
elements.meaning: The speaker asks themselves questions.
elements.try: Ask yourself the question out loud.

speaker.question: What must the speaker know to deliver the line of reasoning toward a decision?
speaker.answer: The speaker must keep the goal in view while voicing each step, its test and its result. Donald Schön calls this reflection in action, where the thinker tries a move, sees what happens and adjusts. George Pólya's heuristics show the shape: understand, plan, try, look back, and the listener receives the reasoning when each check and correction is spoken.

elements.name: Testing
elements.meaning: Each option is tested against a condition.
elements.try: Test each option out loud with if and then.

cue.re: \b(?:if (?:the|i|we|it)|then the|then i|that would|that won'?t|would be right|might be)\b

elements.name: Self Correction
elements.meaning: The speaker catches and corrects a mistake.
elements.try: Say no, wait, when you catch a mistake, and name the fix.

cue.re: \b(?:wait|no,? (?:that|wait)|actually|hold on|that won'?t work|not quite|on second thought)\b

elements.name: Checking
elements.meaning: The speaker checks before deciding.
elements.try: Say let me check, and check.

elements.name: Decision
elements.meaning: The reasoning arrives at a choice.
elements.try: End with what you have decided and why.

cue.re: \b(?:i'?ll|i will|so i|okay,? so|i decide|before i decide|then the total|that'?s it|the answer)\b

elements.name: Reason Markers
elements.meaning: Because and so link the steps.
elements.try: Join your steps with because and so.

absorption.question: Which elements of thinking aloud and of the problem chosen most draw a listener into the reasoning?
absorption.answer: Listeners are drawn in by suspense: a real problem with an uncertain answer, voiced as it unfolds. Wallace Chafe shows that hesitations and false starts mark the edge of consciousness at work, and hearing them invites the listener to think alongside. A problem with a felt stake, a train to catch or a sum that must balance, gives the listener a reason to stay.

elements.name: Hesitation
elements.meaning: Fillers and pauses show thought in motion.
elements.try: Let your hesitations stay audible instead of smoothing them out.

elements.name: Suspense
elements.meaning: The answer stays uncertain while options are weighed.
elements.try: Hold off the answer while you weigh the options aloud.

elements.name: Stakes
elements.meaning: A practical consequence gives the problem weight.
elements.try: Name what happens if you get it wrong.

elements.name: Turns of Mind
elements.meaning: Reversals show the mind turning.
elements.try: Let your reasoning turn on actually or but.

elements.name: Quick Steps
elements.meaning: Short broken sentences track fast thought.
elements.try: Let the sentences stay short as thought moves fast.

arc.name: Problem
arc.move: State the problem you are working on.

arc.name: Attempt
arc.move: Try one possibility out loud.

arc.name: Test

sources: William James, The Principles of Psychology (thought as a stream with substantive and transitive parts)
Dorothy Richardson, Pilgrimage (the first sustained English novel of the stream)
Virginia Woolf, Modern Fiction (the mind receiving a myriad impressions)
Walter Ong, Orality and Literacy (additive rather than subordinative style)
Pauline Oliveros, Deep Listening (attention that includes everything at once)

listener.question: What must a listener bring to follow a mind as it moves from one impression to the next?
listener.answer: William James described thought as a stream with resting places and flights, and the listener follows it best by riding the flights rather than waiting for a thesis. Ong names the additive style of oral speech, the "and, and, and", and a listener who accepts that chain hears association as the organizing logic. It helps to hold a present scene steady in mind, because the stream returns to it between excursions into memory.

elements.name: Present Scene
elements.meaning: A here and now the mind keeps returning to anchors the drift.
elements.try: Name what is in front of you right now, the cup, the window, the sound outside.

elements.name: Additive Chain
elements.meaning: Clauses joined by "and" rather than "because" let the listener move with the mind instead of ahead of it.
elements.try: Let one image lead to the next with "and", without explaining why they follow.

elements.name: A Mind Inside
elements.meaning: An "I" who thinks and keeps thinking gives the stream a consciousness to belong to.
elements.try: Say what you keep thinking of, in the first person, as it arrives.

elements.name: Memory Drift
elements.meaning: The mind slips from the present into a remembered moment and back without announcing it.
elements.try: Let a remembered summer or a person drift in mid-sentence, without a "once" or a "back then".

cue.re: \b(?:the one from|that summer|the summer|when i was|my mother|my father|years ago|as a child)\b

elements.name: Long Breath
elements.meaning: Sentences that run long without a full stop let the listener feel the flow of thought.
elements.try: Keep going past where you would usually stop, joining the next thought with a comma.

speaker.question: What must the speaker know to let a stream of thought carry its feeling without stating it?
speaker.answer: Woolf asked writers to record the atoms as they fall, and the speaker delivers meaning through which impressions return rather than through a stated point. James observed that the transitive parts of thought, the "and" and the "if", carry as much feeling as the nouns, so the speaker trusts the joins. A recurring image becomes the quiet meaning of the stream, the way a motif works in music.

elements.name: Recurring Image
elements.meaning: An image or phrase that comes back carries the feeling the speaker never names.
elements.try: Let one image return two or three times as the thoughts move around it.

elements.name: Echoed Phrase
elements.meaning: Repeating a just-said word, as in "late, it is always late", lets a feeling surface by insistence.
elements.try: Repeat a word you just said and add one thing to it.

elements.name: Sensory Texture
elements.meaning: Colour, temperature and sound give the stream a body for its feeling.
elements.try: Name a colour, a temperature or a sound as it reaches you.

elements.name: Equal Clauses
elements.meaning: Clauses set side by side with commas keep every thought at the same weight, which is the speaker's honesty.
elements.try: Set thoughts side by side with commas instead of ranking them with "because" or "although".

elements.name: Present Tense
elements.meaning: The present tense keeps the speaker inside the moment of thinking.
elements.try: Speak in the present tense, as if the thoughts are happening now.

absorption.question: Which elements of a stream of consciousness draw a listener into the drift of another mind?
absorption.answer: Erickson used long, linked sentences and sensory detail to lead attention inward, and the stream of consciousness does the same by never pausing for argument. Oliveros taught listening that includes every sound at once, and a stream that lets the bus, the light and a memory share one breath invites that open attention. The listener is absorbed when the joins are soft and the images are concrete.

elements.name: Linked Breath
elements.meaning: A long run of "and" keeps the listener moving without a place to step out.
elements.try: Join your next five thoughts with "and", in one breath.

elements.name: Concrete Images
elements.meaning: Plain things seen and felt hold attention gently.
elements.try: Name small concrete things: a cup, a window, an umbrella, a light.

elements.name: Colour and Light
elements.meaning: Naming the quality of light pulls the listener into a visual reverie.
elements.try: Say what colour the light is.

elements.name: Few Full Stops
elements.meaning: Few sentence breaks make the passage feel like one continuous thought.
elements.try: Let your sentences run long and stop rarely.

elements.name: Return of Mood
elements.meaning: Words such as "again" and "always" let a familiar feeling come round like a tide.
elements.try: Notice what is happening again and say so.

arc.name: Anchor
arc.move: Anchor in what is in front of you now.

arc.name: Drift

arc.move: Let one thing lead to the next.

arc.name: Return
arc.move: Come back to the first image.

sources: Walter Ong, Orality and Literacy (the voice reanimating written, subordinative prose)
Alberto Manguel, A History of Reading (reading aloud as a shared act)
Ruth Finnegan, Oral Poetry (performance as part of the text)
Dell Hymes, In Vain I Tried to Tell You (lines and verses within prose)
Walter Benjamin, The Storyteller (the novel and the told tale)

listener.question: What must a listener bring to hear a written text read aloud?
listener.answer: Ong observed that written prose is subordinative, built of long sentences with clauses nested inside clauses, and the listener needs patience to hold a clause open until it closes. Manguel describes reading aloud as a shared act in which the listener lends the reader their trust. A listener appreciates it most by hearing the author's voice behind the reader's, including the formal words, the narrator's asides and the measured pace of the page.

elements.name: Framing Heading
elements.meaning: A chapter title or a named author tells the listener a written text is being voiced.
elements.try: Announce the chapter or the author before you begin.

elements.name: Formal Diction
elements.meaning: Literary words such as "however", "whom" and "obliged" mark the voice of the page.
elements.try: Keep the author's formal words exactly as written.

elements.name: Nested Clauses
elements.meaning: Long sentences with clauses inside them ask the listener to hold a thought open.
elements.try: Read the long sentence through without breaking it, letting the voice carry the clause.

elements.name: Narrator's Distance
elements.meaning: A third-person narrator speaking of "the family" or "it" places the listener outside the scene, looking in.
elements.try: Let the narrator describe from a distance in the third person.

elements.name: Past Record
elements.meaning: A settled past tense tells the listener the events are already written down.
elements.try: Keep the past tense of the text steady.

speaker.question: What must the reader know to deliver an author's voice and syntax faithfully?
speaker.answer: Finnegan shows that performance is part of the text, so the reader must know where each sentence goes before voicing it, to place stress on the main verb and let subordinate clauses fall. Hymes found lines and verses hiding inside prose, and a reader who hears those measures can pace them. The meaning belongs to the author, so the reader serves the syntax and lets the narrator's irony and judgement arrive through tone.

elements.name: Sentence Shape
elements.meaning: Knowing where a long sentence lands lets the reader carry it to its end.
elements.try: Look ahead to where the sentence ends and aim your voice there.

elements.name: Narrator's Judgement
elements.meaning: Phrases such as "however sensible it may have appeared" carry the author's irony.
elements.try: Give the narrator's judging phrases a lighter, knowing tone.

elements.name: Period Detail
elements.meaning: Words of custom and era place the text in its time.
elements.try: Read the words of the period plainly and let them set the age.

cue.re: \b(?:in those days|the custom|generations?|magistrates?|inherit\w*|estate|the family|by the time of|fortunes?)\b

elements.name: Orderly Past Tense
elements.meaning: A consistent past tense marks the reading as record rather than live speech.
elements.try: Keep every verb in the text's own tense.

elements.name: Heading Voice
elements.meaning: Reading the chapter heading in a separate tone frames what follows.
elements.try: Pause after the heading and begin the text in a fresh breath.

absorption.question: Which elements of reading aloud let a listener sink into the world of the page?
absorption.answer: Benjamin wrote that the listener to a tale is in the company of the teller, and reading aloud restores that company to printed prose. An even, unhurried pace and long, well-formed sentences work like the rhythm Erickson used to settle attention. Description of a place that stands still, a house, a lane, a room, gives the listener somewhere to rest while the voice continues.

elements.name: Still Setting
elements.meaning: A described place that holds still gives the mind a room to sit in.
elements.try: Linger on the description of the place before the action begins.

cue.re: \b(?:the house|a house|the lane|the room|the hall|the mill|windows?|the end of|stood at|belonged to)\b

elements.name: Measured Length
elements.meaning: Long sentences read at an even pace lull the listener into the text's time.
elements.try: Slow down and give each long sentence its full length.

elements.name: Omniscient Voice
elements.meaning: A narrator who knows generations of history invites the listener to trust and follow.
elements.try: Let the narrator's knowledge of the past carry the listener.

cue.re: \b(?:for (?:four|three|many|several) generations|in those days|it was the custom|by the time|had belonged|each had)\b

elements.name: Third-Person World
elements.meaning: Characters seen from outside let the listener watch a whole world unfold.
elements.try: Describe the people of the text from the narrator's distance.

elements.name: Literary Cadence
elements.meaning: Balanced, formal phrasing has its own cadence that rocks the ear.
elements.try: Let the formal phrasing set the rise and fall of your voice.

arc.name: Heading
arc.move: Give the heading or the author.

arc.name: Setting
arc.move: Read the setting slowly.

arc.name: Development
arc.move: Carry the long sentence through to its end.

arc.name: Close

cue.re: \b(?:the end|end of (?:the )?chapter|and so|thus it was|from that day)\b

arc.move: Read the closing line and let it rest.

listener.question: What must a listener bring to join a song as it is sung?
listener.answer: Finnegan reminds us that song is a performance in which the audience often takes part, so the listener comes ready to sing along, clap or answer. Blacking argued that music is a shared bodily activity, and the listener appreciates a song through the body, by keeping time. Knowing the chorus is coming, because the singer says so, lets the listener lean toward it.

elements.name: Call to Join
elements.meaning: An invitation such as "sing it with me" turns listeners into singers.
elements.try: Invite everyone in: say "sing it with me" before the chorus.

cue.re: \b(?:sing (?:it )?with me|everybody|all together|join in|sing along|clap|come on|with me now)\b

elements.name: Vocables
elements.meaning: Syllables such as "la la" and "oh oh" carry the tune without words to understand.
elements.try: Sing a line on "la la la" or "oh oh" so anyone can join.

elements.name: Chorus Signpost
elements.meaning: Naming the chorus or the verse tells the listener where they are in the song.
elements.try: Say "here comes the chorus" so the listener can find it.

elements.name: Group Voice
elements.meaning: A shared "we" makes the song belong to the room.
elements.try: Sing "we" so the song belongs to everyone.

elements.name: Sung Commands
elements.meaning: Short commands like "hold that note" lead the group through the song.
elements.try: Lead with a short command: hold it, bring it round, sing out.

speaker.question: What must the singer know to deliver a song's feeling and bring the group with them?
speaker.answer: Lord showed that the singer composes in performance from formulas, so the song leader must know the returning lines well enough to call them at the right moment. In the Child ballads, refrain and incremental repetition carry the meaning, and the singer delivers feeling by returning to the same line with more force. The singer also knows how to lead the group in, much as a hymn leader lines out each phrase in common metre.

elements.name: Refrain Return
elements.meaning: A line that comes back carries the song's heart.
elements.try: Bring the main line back one more time, a little stronger.

elements.name: Lining Out
elements.meaning: Calling the next line or action before the group sings it leads them as hymn leaders do.
elements.try: Call the next line before the group sings it.

cue.re: \b(?:sing it|hold that note|bring it|one more time|everybody sing|now|again)\b

elements.name: Vocable Hook
elements.meaning: A hook sung on open syllables is easy for anyone to carry.
elements.try: Make the hook a run of open syllables like "oh oh oh".

elements.name: Out Loud
elements.meaning: Naming the volume and the togetherness gives the group permission to be loud.
elements.try: Ask the room to sing it out loud together.

elements.name: Formula Lines
elements.meaning: Stock phrases such as "one more time" are the formulas a song leader relies on.
elements.try: Use a stock song phrase like "one more time" to carry the group.

cue.re: \b(?:one more time|round again|from the top|take it home|here we go)\b

absorption.question: Which elements of singing together draw a group into a shared trance?
absorption.answer: Erickson used repetition and rhythm to lead attention, and group song does this with every returning chorus. Blacking described the trance of communal music in which bodies keep one time, and Oliveros taught listening to sound for its own sake, which vocables invite. The more the song repeats and the more voices join, the deeper the shared absorption.

elements.name: Repetition Loop
elements.meaning: Repeated lines and sounds lull the group into one pulse.
elements.try: Repeat the chorus until the room sings it without you.

elements.name: Open Syllables
elements.meaning: Wordless syllables free the mind from meaning so the body takes the song.
elements.try: Drop the words and sing the tune on "la".

elements.name: Many Voices
elements.meaning: Everybody singing at once dissolves the listener into the group.
elements.try: Bring every voice in at once.

elements.name: Held Note
elements.meaning: A sustained note suspends time and breath.
elements.try: Hold one note longer than feels usual.

elements.name: Circling Back
elements.meaning: Going "round again" makes the song a circle that is easy to stay inside.
elements.try: Bring it round again from the top.

cue.re: \b(?:round again|comes back|back round|once more|one more time|again)\b

Milton H. Erickson, Hypnotic Realities (repetition and embedded suggestion)

listener.question: What must a listener bring to feel the words of a song lyric?
listener.answer: Frye described the lyric as speech overheard, addressed to a "you" the listener can step into. Frith observed that popular song works through the singer's voice and a person addressed, so the listener appreciates a lyric by imagining themselves as the one sung to or the one singing. A listener who knows the hook is coming hears each verse as a road back to it.

elements.name: Addressed You
elements.meaning: A beloved "you" lets every listener stand in the place of the one sung to.
elements.try: Sing the line straight to "you".

cue.re: \b(?:you'?re the one|to you|for you|with you|back to you|about you|without you)\b

elements.name: Hook Phrase
elements.meaning: A short phrase repeated at once fixes the song in memory.
elements.try: Say your hook twice in a row.

elements.name: Song Vocabulary
elements.meaning: Familiar words of popular song such as "baby", "forever" and "tonight" signal the lyric genre.
elements.try: Reach for the plain words of song: tonight, forever, always.

cue.re: \b(?:baby|forever|tonight|always|my heart|every time|hold me|don'?t let go|the one|the night)\b

elements.name: I to You
elements.meaning: An "I" singing to a "you" sets up the intimate scene of the lyric.
elements.try: Put "I" and "you" in the same line.

elements.name: End Rhyme
elements.meaning: Rhymes at the ends of phrases, such as "long" and "song", tell the ear a line is complete.
elements.try: End two phrases on words that rhyme.

speaker.question: What must the singer know to deliver a lyric's hook and feeling?
speaker.answer: In the ballad tradition, incremental repetition changes one word of a returning line so the feeling grows, and the lyricist knows which word to turn. Erickson showed how a phrase repeated and slightly varied carries an embedded suggestion, which is what a hook does. The singer must know the single feeling the lyric holds, a promise or a longing, and return every verse to it.

elements.name: The Promise
elements.meaning: A vow such as "I will always" states the lyric's single feeling.
elements.try: State the promise plainly: I will always, I will never let go.

cue.re: \b(?:i will always|i'?ll always|i will never|i'?ll be|forever|always come back|still about you)\b

elements.name: Incremental Repeat
elements.meaning: A line returned with one word changed lets the feeling grow.
elements.try: Repeat your hook and change one word.

elements.name: Night and Road
elements.meaning: Images of night, road and time frame the longing.
elements.try: Place the feeling in a night, a road, or a time of day.

cue.re: \b(?:when the night|the road|the night|every time|tonight|all night|long)\b

elements.name: One Listener
elements.meaning: Keeping the words on one "you" holds the lyric's intimacy.
elements.try: Keep every line pointed at one "you".

elements.name: This Song
elements.meaning: A lyric that names itself, "this song", folds the performance into the meaning.
elements.try: Let the song name itself: every time I sing this song.

absorption.question: Which elements of a lyric draw the listener into its feeling?
absorption.answer: Repetition and rhythm, the core of Erickson's trance language, are the lyric's own devices, and a hook repeated across verses lulls attention onto the feeling. Frith noted that listeners take up the "you" of a song as their own, which deepens absorption through identification. Rhyme and a steady line length let the ear predict and settle.

elements.name: Hook Loop
elements.meaning: The hook returning again and again becomes a gentle loop for the mind.
elements.try: Return to the hook after every few lines.

elements.name: Identification
elements.meaning: A "you" the listener can occupy draws them inside the song.
elements.try: Address the listener as "you" so they become the one sung to.

elements.name: Rhyme
elements.meaning: Rhyme lets the ear predict the line's end and relax into it.
elements.try: Close two lines with a rhyme.

elements.name: Longing
elements.meaning: A held longing or return gives the absorption an emotional pull.
elements.try: Name what you long to come back to.

elements.name: I and You
elements.meaning: The bond between an "I" and a "you" makes the song a private room.
elements.try: Keep "I" and "you" close together in each line.

listener.question: What must a listener bring to receive a poem spoken aloud?
listener.answer: Aristotle held that the gift of metaphor is seeing likeness in unlike things, and the listener appreciates a poem by letting one thing stand for another, a moon for a wound, a wind for a scholar. Hymes showed that oral poetry is organized in lines and measures, so the listener hears the line breaks in the breath. A poem rewards a listener who lets images arrive without asking for their argument.

elements.name: Metaphor
elements.meaning: One thing named as another asks the listener to hold two images at once.
elements.try: Say what one thing is, as if it were another: the moon is a wound.

elements.name: Simile
elements.meaning: A likeness spoken with "like" or "as" opens the image gently.
elements.try: Compare one thing to another with "like" or "as if".

elements.name: Line Breath
elements.meaning: Short measured phrases mark the lines of the poem.
elements.try: Speak in short lines and breathe at each break.

elements.name: Images
elements.meaning: Concrete sensory words carry the poem's meaning to the senses.
elements.try: Name what can be seen, heard or touched.

elements.name: Personification
elements.meaning: Things of nature given human acts, a willow that reads, invite empathy with the world.
elements.try: Let something in nature do what a person does.

speaker.question: What must the poet know to deliver a poem's image and its turn?
speaker.answer: Finnegan shows that the meaning of an oral poem lives in its performance, so the poet must know where the image lands and where the poem turns. The turn, the volta of the sonnet tradition, is the moment the image opens into feeling, and the poet slows into it. Ong observes that sound patterns aid memory, so alliteration, assonance and repeated structure carry the meaning to the ear.

elements.name: Central Image
elements.meaning: One governing image holds the poem together.
elements.try: Choose one image and let every line touch it.

elements.name: The Turn
elements.meaning: A turn such as "and the" or "yet" moves the image into feeling.
elements.try: Turn the poem with "yet" or "and then" toward what the image means.

elements.name: Sound Pattern
elements.meaning: Alliteration and repeated sounds carry the line in the ear.
elements.try: Let two neighbouring words begin with the same sound.

elements.name: Compression
elements.meaning: Few words per line press meaning into each word.
elements.try: Cut your line to its strongest words.

elements.name: Lyric Heart
elements.meaning: A quiet first person, "my heart", gives the image an inner life.
elements.try: Let the image touch your own heart once.

cue.re: \b(?:my heart|my soul|we gave|our names|i hold|my memory)\b

absorption.question: Which elements of a spoken poem draw the listener into reverie?
absorption.answer: Bachelard described the poetic image as a call to reverie, a still moment in which the listener dwells inside the image. Erickson used sensory detail, rhythm and slowness to lead attention inward, and a poem spoken with measured lines and rich images does the same. Personified nature, the tide that sleeps, softens the boundary between listener and world.

elements.name: Reverie Image
elements.meaning: A still, luminous image invites the listener to dwell rather than follow.
elements.try: Hold one image long enough for the listener to rest in it.

elements.name: Slow Rhythm
elements.meaning: Even, measured phrases slow the breath.
elements.try: Slow down and give each phrase the same length.

elements.name: Hush and Sleep
elements.meaning: Words of quiet and rest suggest stillness to the listener.
elements.try: Bring in a word of quiet: hush, sleep, still.

elements.name: Living Nature
elements.meaning: Nature that breathes and sleeps draws the listener into the scene.
elements.try: Let the sea or the wind act like a living thing.

elements.name: Sensory Density
elements.meaning: Many sensory words close together fill the listener's inner senses.
elements.try: Name colours and textures in each line.

arc.name: Image
arc.move: Give one concrete image.

arc.name: Extension
arc.move: Extend the image one step further.

arc.name: Turn
arc.move: Turn the poem with but or yet.

arc.name: Closing Image
arc.move: End on a still image.

listener.question: What must a listener bring to follow a story and feel its pull?
listener.answer: Labov found that told stories open with an orientation, who, where and when, and the listener needs that ground before the action can matter. Bruner calls narrative a mode of thought about intention and its trouble, so the listener brings a readiness to care what a character wants. Formulaic openings such as "once there was" tell the listener to set aside the present and enter the tale.

elements.name: Opening Formula
elements.meaning: A formula such as "once there was" signals that a tale begins.
elements.try: Begin with "once there was" or "one morning".

cue.re: \b(?:once upon a time|once there was|once there lived|long ago|one (?:day|morning|night|evening)|there once was)\b

elements.name: Orientation
elements.meaning: A character placed in a setting gives the listener someone to follow.
elements.try: Say who it is and where they live before anything happens.

elements.name: Protagonist
elements.meaning: A third-person hero, "she" or "he", carries the listener through events.
elements.try: Keep one character at the centre and follow what they do.

elements.name: Past Narration
elements.meaning: The narrative past tense tells the listener these events have happened.
elements.try: Tell it in the past tense, as something that happened.

elements.name: Time Markers
elements.meaning: Markers such as "when", "then" and "finally" let the listener track time.
elements.try: Mark each step of time with "then" or "when".

speaker.question: What must the storyteller know to deliver the moral within the story?
speaker.answer: Benjamin wrote that every real story carries counsel, something useful, woven into the events rather than stated, and the teller must know that counsel before beginning. In Labov's terms the evaluation tells the listener why the story is worth telling, and the resolution and coda bring the moral home to the present. The teller delivers the moral through the change in the character, so the turning point must be clear.

elements.name: Complicating Action
elements.meaning: A sequence of acts that raises a question drives the story forward.
elements.try: Give your character something to do that changes their situation.

elements.name: Turning Point
elements.meaning: A moment such as "for the first time" marks the change that holds the meaning.
elements.try: Mark the turn: "and for the first time" or "then everything changed".

cue.re: \b(?:for the first time|suddenly|but then|everything changed|at last|finally|in that moment)\b

elements.name: Resolution
elements.meaning: An ending that settles the action lets the moral land.
elements.try: Close the action: say how it ended and where they went.

cue.re: \b(?:turned (?:back )?(?:toward|for) home|went home|came home|ever after|from then on|in the end|and so)\b

elements.name: Evaluation
elements.meaning: Feeling words and emphasis tell the listener why this matters.
elements.try: Say how it felt, so the listener knows why the story matters.

elements.name: Moral
elements.meaning: A spoken lesson, "and that is why", states the counsel the story carries.
elements.try: If you wish, say plainly what the story teaches: "and that is why".

cue.re: \b(?:that is why|the moral|the lesson|and so (?:it is|we)|teaches us|ever since)\b

absorption.question: Which elements of telling, and of choosing the story, draw the listener into the tale?
absorption.answer: Green and Brock call it transportation, the sense of being carried into a story world, and it deepens with vivid scenes, a character to identify with and a suspense of what comes next. Gerrig adds that listeners participate by filling gaps and anticipating. A teller who moves step by step through concrete places, past the mill, past the bridge, uses the same pacing and leading Erickson used to deepen attention.

elements.name: Journey
elements.meaning: Movement through named places carries the listener along with the hero.

sources: E. M. Forster, Aspects of the Novel (flat and round characters)
Aristotle, Poetics (character revealed through choice, and the tragic flaw)
Jerome Bruner, Actual Minds, Possible Worlds (the landscape of consciousness)
Joseph Campbell, The Hero with a Thousand Faces (transformation of the hero)
Lisa Zunshine, Why We Read Fiction (theory of mind in narrative)

listener.question: What must a listener bring to follow a character's change?
listener.answer: Forster called a character round when it can surprise us convincingly, and the listener appreciates development by remembering who the character was so the change can register. Bruner describes the landscape of consciousness that runs beside the landscape of action, so the listener attends to fears, wants and pride as much as to events. Zunshine shows that we enjoy tracking minds, so the listener brings a readiness to infer motive.

elements.name: Inner State
elements.meaning: Named fears, wants and pride give the listener a mind to track.
elements.try: Name what the character fears or wants.

elements.name: Starting Trait
elements.meaning: A trait stated at the outset gives the change a starting point.
elements.try: Say what the character was like at the start.

elements.name: Character Focus
elements.meaning: A steady "she" or "he" keeps the listener with one person.
elements.try: Keep the focus on one character throughout.

elements.name: Motive
elements.meaning: Links between feeling and act, "that fear made her cruel", show why the character acts.
elements.try: Connect a feeling to what it made the character do.

elements.name: Relationships
elements.meaning: A brother, mother or friend reveals character in relation to others.
elements.try: Show the character with someone they love or resist.

speaker.question: What must the speaker know to deliver the arc of a character's change?
speaker.answer: Aristotle held that character is revealed through choice, so the speaker must know the decision that shows who the character becomes. The arc moves from a flaw to its transformation, the movement Campbell traced through the hero's return, and the speaker marks its beginning, its pressure and its end. Time markers such as "as the winter went on" and "by spring" let the listener feel the change take time.

elements.name: Arc of Change
elements.meaning: Words of becoming, "became", "grew", "turned into", state the change itself.
elements.try: Say what the character became.

elements.name: The Flaw
elements.meaning: A named weakness gives the arc something to overcome.
elements.try: Name the character's flaw out loud.

elements.name: Pressure
elements.meaning: A "but" that sets loyalty against pride shows the conflict that forces change.
elements.try: Set two of the character's values against each other with "but".

elements.name: Passage of Time
elements.meaning: Seasons and stages show that change takes time.
elements.try: Mark time passing: as the winter went on, by spring.

cue.re: \b(?:as the (?:winter|summer|years?|months?|days?) went on|by (?:spring|summer|autumn|winter|the end)|over the years|in time|years later)\b

elements.name: Revealing Choice
elements.meaning: A decision, someone who stayed, reveals who the character now is.
elements.try: Show the character choosing, and let the choice speak.

absorption.question: Which elements of telling a character's change draw the listener into that person's life?
absorption.answer: Green and Brock found that identification with a character deepens transportation, and a listener absorbed in a character feels the change as their own. Erickson's pacing and leading applies here, matching the listener's experience of fear or pride before leading them toward strength. A clear before and after, held across seasons, gives the listener a slow arc to settle into.

elements.name: Shared Feeling
elements.meaning: Feelings any listener knows, fear and loyalty, invite identification.
elements.try: Name a feeling every listener has known.

elements.name: Before and After
elements.meaning: A visible contrast between old and new self rewards the listener's attention.
elements.try: Say plainly who the character was and who they became.

elements.name: Slow Seasons
elements.meaning: Seasons turning give the change a slow, absorbing rhythm.
elements.try: Let the seasons turn while the character changes.

elements.name: Strength Found
elements.meaning: The flaw becoming strength gives the listener a moment of release.
elements.try: Let the flaw turn into a strength at the end.

elements.name: Close Third Person
elements.meaning: Staying close inside "she" lets the listener live in the character.
elements.try: Stay inside your character's feelings in the third person.

arc.name: Pressure

arc.name: Change

Gaston Bachelard, The Poetics of Space (the felt interiority of places)
Keith Basso, Wisdom Sits in Places (Western Apache placenames that hold stories)
Milton Erickson, as recorded in Haley's Uncommon Therapy (sensory detail and pacing in trance language)
Pauline Oliveros, Deep Listening (attention to the whole field of sound)

listener.question: What must a listener bring to see a place through spoken words?
listener.answer: A listener brings a store of remembered places, and Yi-Fu Tuan shows that space becomes place through the attention a person gives it. The words call up the listener's own valleys and streets, so the listener needs a willingness to build the scene inwardly from each named feature. Keith Basso found among the Western Apache that a named place carries its whole history, and even a stranger's description works best when the listener can place each feature in relation to the others.

elements.name: Named Features
elements.meaning: The listener receives concrete features of land, water or town to build the scene from.
elements.try: Name two or three concrete features of the place, such as a river, a ridge or a square.

elements.name: Spatial Orientation
elements.meaning: Words of position tell the listener where each feature stands in relation to the others.
elements.try: Place each feature with a word of position, such as below, beyond or across.

elements.name: A Vantage Point
elements.meaning: A viewer stands somewhere in the scene, so the listener knows where to stand too.
elements.try: Say where you are standing as you look, so the listener stands there with you.

cue.re: \b(?:below us|before us|around us|we stood|i stood|from (?:the|here|where)|looking (?:out|down|up)|in front of|at our feet|opened (?:below|before))\b

elements.name: Time and Weather
elements.meaning: The hour and the weather set the light the listener sees by.
elements.try: Tell the hour or the weather, so the scene has its own light.

elements.name: Near and Far
elements.meaning: The scene moves between near detail and far distance, giving it depth.
elements.try: Move the eye from something close at hand to something on the far horizon.

speaker.question: What must the speaker know to deliver the felt sense of a place?
speaker.answer: The speaker must know the feeling the place holds and choose the details that carry it, because Bachelard shows that a described space is always a felt space. The meaning of scenery lies in mood, so the speaker selects light, sound and motion that agree with one another. Ordering the details as the eye would travel lets the listener arrive at the feeling without being told it.

elements.name: A Dominant Mood
elements.meaning: The details agree on one feeling, such as calm, menace or longing.
elements.try: Choose one feeling for the place and keep every detail in its key.

elements.name: The Eye's Path
elements.meaning: The description travels in an order the eye could follow, from one feature to the next.
elements.try: Lead the eye in one direction, from near to far or from ground to sky.

elements.name: Living Motion
elements.meaning: The land seems to move or breathe through verbs of winding, hanging and opening.
elements.try: Give the land a verb, so the river winds and the mist hangs.

elements.name: Quality of Light
elements.meaning: The particular light of the moment colours the whole place.
elements.try: Describe how the light falls and what it touches.

elements.name: Beyond the Eye
elements.meaning: Sound, smell and touch reach past what the eye can see.
elements.try: Add one sound or smell that comes from out of sight.

absorption.question: Which elements of a described scene most draw a listener into it?
absorption.answer: Milton Erickson built trance by pacing a listener through sensory detail, one sense after another, until the inner scene feels present. Long, flowing sentences joined by and let the listener drift, and a sound heard somewhere out of sight widens attention the way Pauline Oliveros describes in Deep Listening. Choosing a place with distance and weather in it gives the imagination room to travel.

elements.name: Sensory Layering
elements.meaning: Sight, sound, smell and touch arrive one after another and fill the scene.
elements.try: Move through the senses, adding what is heard and smelled after what is seen.

elements.name: Flowing Sentences
elements.meaning: Long sentences joined by and and commas carry the listener along without a break.
elements.try: Let one sentence run on with and, carrying the eye across the land.

elements.name: A Distant Sound
elements.meaning: A sound from somewhere unseen widens the listener's attention to the whole field.
elements.try: Let a bell, a bird or the wind sound from somewhere out of sight.

elements.name: Atmosphere
elements.meaning: Mist, rain, wind or haze soften the edges and make the scene feel close and dreamlike.
elements.try: Bring in mist, rain or a change of wind.

elements.name: Present Presence
elements.meaning: Stillness words and lingering phrases slow the listener down inside the place.
elements.try: Pause on one still thing and let it rest a moment.

listener.question: What must a listener know to receive the lore of a people or a world?
listener.answer: A listener of lore needs the frame of a community whose customs are being explained, since Ong describes oral knowledge as kept for the group and tied to its life. The names of houses, orders and places become meaningful once the listener accepts that each stands for an inheritance. Jan Vansina shows that oral tradition carries history as lineage and custom, so the listener follows best by holding who belongs to whom and what is owed to whom.

speaker.question: What must the speaker know to hand down the customs and lineage of lore?
speaker.answer: The speaker must know the charter, in Malinowski's sense: which custom the lore justifies and which lineage gives it authority. Lore delivers its meaning by tracing a present practice back to a founder or first event, so the speaker keeps the chain of descent unbroken. Speaking as a keeper of records lends the ethos Aristotle names, because the listener trusts a voice that knows the old accounts.

absorption.question: Which elements of telling lore most draw a listener into another world's order?
absorption.answer: Lore absorbs through the density of a world that holds together, as each new name confirms the ones before it. Parry and Lord showed that formulaic, catalogue-like speech lets listeners settle into a rhythm of recognition, and lore uses lists of houses, oaths and rites in the same way. A ceremonial cadence and a word spoken to the ancestors invite the listener to stand inside the custom as one of its keepers.

elements.try: List the houses, orders or places in a steady sequence.

elements.name: Ritual Words

elements.try: Describe the words or gesture that every keeper makes at the rite.

elements.name: Old Texture

elements.name: A Consistent World

listener.question: What must a listener bring to receive a myth as sacred truth?
listener.answer: A listener of myth enters what Mircea Eliade calls illud tempus, the time of beginnings, and so must accept that the events stand before ordinary history. The listener needs to recognise the great elements, sky, sea, fire and earth, as actors with wills of their own. Levi-Strauss shows that myth thinks in opposed pairs, so a listener appreciates it most by noticing what was one and became two.

elements.name: The Time of Beginnings
elements.meaning: The myth opens in a time before ordinary time, such as in the beginning.
elements.try: Open in the time before time, with in the beginning or long ago.

speaker.question: What must the speaker know to deliver the sacred truth or origin a myth carries?
speaker.answer: The speaker must know which present thing the myth explains, because Malinowski calls myth a charter that justifies how the world and its customs are now. The meaning arrives in the etiological turn, that is why the mountains smoke, which ties the origin to what the listener can still see. Telling it with the authority of the tradition, as handed down, gives the ethos that sacred speech requires.

elements.try: Close by saying what in the world today this story explains, with that is why.

absorption.question: Which elements of telling a myth most draw a listener into sacred time?
absorption.answer: Eliade describes the recitation of myth as a return to the time of origins, and the listener is absorbed when the telling leaves ordinary time behind. Elemental images such as fire hidden in a mountain carry the force of dream, and Campbell notes that these images recur across peoples because they speak to shared depths. The chain of and then, and that is why, gives the cadence of a hymn, and Erickson's repetition and rhythm deepen the same absorption.

elements.name: Elemental Imagery

elements.name: The Chain of And

elements.name: Sacred Vocabulary

elements.try: Use the words of the sacred: the heavens, the holy fire, the gods.

elements.name: Return to Now

elements.try: Bring the story back to the present, to what we still see and do.

elements.name: Timelessness
elements.meaning: Words of always and forever lift the events out of ordinary time.
elements.try: Say what has been so forever, and will always be.

listener.question: What must a listener bring to grasp an account of the order of the cosmos?
listener.answer: A listener of cosmology needs a sense of scale, the willingness to hold billions of years and vast distances as real. Bruner distinguishes the paradigmatic mode of explanation from the narrative mode, and cosmology asks the listener to hold both at once, the law and the unfolding. The listener appreciates it best by treating space, time and matter as characters in one long story, as Carl Sagan taught.

elements.meaning: Words for the universe, stars, galaxies and atoms name the field of the account.

elements.try: Give one number or measure to hold the scale.

elements.name: The First State

elements.try: Describe the first state of everything, before anything formed.

speaker.question: What must the speaker know to deliver the order of the world in a cosmology?
speaker.answer: The speaker must know the sequence and the law: what formed from what, and what governs the whole. Eliade shows that every cosmogony is a model of order emerging from formlessness, and the scientific account keeps that same arc from a hot dense state to galaxies. The meaning is delivered when the speaker places the listener inside the order, so that space and time become characters in the story itself.

elements.name: Unfolding Process

absorption.question: Which elements of telling the cosmos most draw a listener into wonder?
absorption.answer: Cosmology absorbs through scale, and Carl Sagan held audiences by moving from the vast to the intimate and back. A steady, unhurried unfolding of stages works like Erickson's pacing and leading, carrying the listener step by step beyond ordinary sense. Images of light, filaments and voids give the mind something to see in the dark, and the closing turn toward ourselves turns wonder into belonging.

listener.question: What must a listener hold in mind to follow a mystery?
listener.answer: A listener of a mystery holds two stories at once, as Todorov describes: the hidden story of what happened and the told story of finding it out. The listener must remember each clue, each suspect and each contradiction, because the pleasure lies in reasoning toward the answer alongside the teller. Barthes calls this the hermeneutic code, a question posed and its answer held back.

speaker.question: What must the speaker know to deliver the withheld answer of a mystery?
speaker.answer: The speaker must know the answer fully and decide what to withhold, since Barthes shows suspense lives in the delay between the question and its resolution. Each clue must be fair, so the solution feels both surprising and inevitable when it arrives. The speaker places contradictions deliberately, an impossible locked room or an alibi that holds, because these are what turn the listener into an investigator.

elements.try: Give each suspect an alibi or a motive.

absorption.question: Which elements of telling a mystery most hold a listener in suspense?
absorption.answer: A mystery absorbs through suspense, and Peter Brooks calls the desire for the ending the engine of every plot. Erickson used confusion to narrow attention, and a locked room or a contradiction does the same, so the listener leans in to resolve it. Direct questions pull the listener into the search, and the shared we of the investigators makes them a partner in it.

elements.name: Questions Aloud
elements.meaning: Spoken questions draw the listener into the search.
elements.try: Ask the question aloud, as though the listener might answer.

elements.name: The Impossible
elements.meaning: A locked room or a vanished object narrows attention to the puzzle.
elements.try: Make one fact seem impossible, a door locked from the inside.
