sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric (ethos, pathos, logos and the enthymeme)
Stephen Toulmin, The Uses of Argument (claim, data, warrant, backing, rebuttal)
Chaim Perelman and Lucie Olbrechts-Tyteca, The New Rhetoric (argument as adherence of an audience)
Cicero, De Oratore (the parts of an oration and the orator's duties)
Walter Ong, Orality and Literacy (the agonistic tone of oral thought)

listener.question: What must a listener bring to weigh a spoken argument?
listener.answer: A listener of an argument needs to know what is at stake and what is being claimed, because Perelman shows an argument aims at the adherence of a particular audience. The listener weighs the claim against the evidence, so the listener needs the claim stated early and plainly. Aristotle notes that the enthymeme leaves a premise for the audience to supply, so the listener brings shared values for the argument to stand on.

elements.name: A Stated Claim
elements.meaning: The point is announced plainly, so the listener knows what to weigh.
elements.try: State your claim in one plain sentence near the start.

cue.re: \b(?:the point (?:of all of this|is)|my claim|i claim|i argue|i would argue|the case|we should|we must|should|ought to|it is (?:clear|true|wrong|right) that|simple)\b

elements.name: The Stakes
elements.meaning: The listener hears what is gained or lost, in value, cost or fairness.
elements.try: Say what is gained or lost if the listener agrees.

elements.name: Evidence Offered
elements.meaning: Facts, figures or examples are put forward for the listener to judge.
elements.try: Offer one fact, figure or example the listener can judge.

elements.name: Shared Value
elements.meaning: We and should appeal to values the speaker and listener hold in common.
elements.try: Appeal to something we all value, using we.

speaker.question: What must the speaker know to deliver the claim of an argument?
speaker.answer: The speaker must know the claim, the data and the warrant that links them, which Stephen Toulmin set out as the layout of every argument. Anticipating the rebuttal shows the strength of the claim, and Aristotle counts such fairness as part of ethos. The meaning lands when the speaker closes by drawing the conclusion explicitly, with therefore, so the listener carries the claim away.

elements.name: The Warrant
elements.meaning: Because, therefore and it follows tie the evidence to the claim.
elements.try: Link your evidence to your claim with because or therefore.

cue.re: \b(?:because|since|therefore|thus|so we|it follows|which means|that means|hence|consequently|as a result)\b

elements.name: Data
elements.meaning: Specific evidence, figures and studies support the claim.
elements.try: Add one specific figure or study.

elements.name: The Rebuttal
elements.meaning: The speaker names the opposing case and answers it.
elements.try: Name the strongest objection and answer it.

cue.re: \b(?:the case against|critics?|opponents?|some say|some argue|objection|does not hold|doesn't hold|on the other hand|however|admittedly|granted|they claim)\b

elements.name: The Conclusion
elements.meaning: The speaker draws the conclusion out loud.
elements.try: Close by saying what therefore follows, and what we should do.

cue.re: \b(?:in conclusion|to conclude|in short|in sum|the answer is|what it comes down to|therefore|so we should|that is why we)\b

elements.name: The Call
elements.meaning: Should and must turn the claim into a course of action.
elements.try: Say plainly what should be done.

absorption.question: Which elements of making an argument most draw a listener in?
absorption.answer: Argument absorbs through momentum, and Ong notes that oral thought is agonistic, so a clear opponent and a clear stake hold attention. Short, declarative sentences and parallel structures give the rhythm of the classical orator, and Cicero's repetitions build toward a peroration. The feeling of a case closing, step by step, works like Erickson's pacing and leading: each agreed point carries the listener to the next.

elements.name: Declarative Punch
elements.meaning: Short, plain sentences land each point with force.
elements.try: Say the point again in a short, plain sentence.

elements.name: The Opponent
elements.meaning: A named opposing case gives the argument a contest to win.
elements.try: Name who disagrees and why they are wrong.

cue.re: \b(?:the case against|critics?|opponents?|some say|some argue|objection|does not hold|doesn't hold|on the other hand|however|admittedly|granted|they claim)\b

elements.name: Stepwise Case
elements.meaning: Each step follows from the last until the conclusion feels inevitable.
elements.try: Build the case in steps, each one following from the last.

elements.name: Parallelism
elements.meaning: Repeated structures build rhythm and weight.
elements.try: Repeat a sentence pattern three times, changing only the end.

elements.name: Certainty
elements.meaning: Words of certainty, clear and simple, carry conviction.
elements.try: Speak with certainty: say what is clear and what does not hold.
